title: Projects vs business as usual
blurb: State the differences between a project and business as usual, and see how projects hand over into BAU.
question: Castlegate Bank processes thousands of payments every day. This year it is also replacing its mobile banking app. Which of these is business as usual, which is a project, and what are the differences between them?

teach.h: Two kinds of work in every organisation
teach.body: Every organisation does two kinds of work. Business as usual (BAU) keeps it running today. Projects change it for tomorrow. A supermarket serving customers and restocking shelves is doing BAU. Refitting the store with self-service tills is a project. The PFQ expects you to state the differences between the two clearly, and to spot which is which in a short scenario.

Business as usual is the ongoing, repetitive operations that run the organisation: its steady state. Think payroll, customer service, manufacturing, invoicing. BAU aims for stability and efficiency, is carried out by permanent functional teams (finance, HR, operations), and carries lower risk because the work is well understood and repeated. In plain English: BAU is 'the day job'.

teach.h: Project vs BAU, side by side
teach.caption: Learn these six rows. Almost every exam question on this outcome is one of them, sometimes reversed to catch you out.

teach.h: BAU is a loop that keeps turning
teach.caption: Payroll runs the same way month after month, by the same team, with no finish line. That repetition is the signature of BAU.

teach.text: Budgets, deadlines, targets and benefits are NOT what separate projects from BAU: both have them. A distractor such as 'projects have tightly controlled budgets, BAU does not' is wrong. The real difference: projects drive change; BAU continues existing activities.

teach.body: Projects and BAU are partners, not rivals. A project creates its outputs and then hands them into BAU, a step called transition. BAU then uses those outputs every day, and that is where most benefits are actually realised. Castlegate Bank's app replacement is a project. Once the new app is live, supporting customers who use it becomes part of BAU.

teach.h: Castlegate Bank: from BAU, through a project, back to BAU

steps.label: Project
steps.sub: Build and test the new app

steps.label: Transition
steps.sub: Train staff, migrate users, go live

steps.label: BAU tomorrow
steps.sub: Support customers on the new app

teach.caption: The project ends at transition; the change it made carries on inside BAU.

head: Project
Business as usual
teach.caption: Treat a unique piece of change like routine work and it tends to drift: it needs the structure that project management provides.

rows.label: The annual audit of the accounts

teach.note: Happening only once a year does not make something a project. The annual audit follows the same routine every time, so it is BAU.

items: BAU is the ongoing, repetitive operations that run the organisation (steady state).
Projects are temporary, unique and deliver change; BAU is ongoing, repetitive and aims for stability.
Projects carry more uncertainty and use temporary teams; BAU uses permanent functional teams.
Projects hand their outputs into BAU (transition), and BAU then realises most of the benefits.

summary: You can now state the differences between a project and business as usual: temporary versus ongoing, unique versus repetitive, change versus stability, higher versus lower risk, temporary versus permanent teams. You can also explain how projects hand their outputs into BAU so benefits can be realised.

A.q: Which of the following best describes business as usual?
options: Ongoing, repeated operations that run the business
A temporary effort that delivers a unique, new output
The coordination of related projects for benefits
The selection and prioritisation of change work
A.why: BAU is the ongoing, repetitive operations that keep the organisation running in its steady state.

whyNot.1: A temporary effort delivering a unique output is a project.
whyNot.2: Coordinating related projects to deliver benefits is programme management.
whyNot.3: Selecting and prioritising change work is portfolio management.

A.q: Compared with business as usual, project work typically involves…
options: more repetition
a permanent team
more uncertainty
no fixed end date
A.why: Project work is unique, so it carries more uncertainty (risk) than well-practised routine work.

whyNot.0: Repetition is a feature of BAU, not projects.
whyNot.1: Projects use temporary teams; permanent teams belong to BAU.
whyNot.3: Projects are temporary with a defined end; it is BAU that has no planned end.

A.q: A new manager asks what fundamentally separates projects from BAU. What is the best answer?
options: Projects have budgets; BAU work carries no cost at all
Projects have benefits; BAU work creates no real value
Projects have deadlines; BAU work never has any targets
Projects deliver change; BAU keeps operations running
A.why: The fundamental difference is purpose: projects drive change, while BAU continues the existing activities of the organisation.

whyNot.0: BAU has budgets and costs too, so this is not a difference.
whyNot.1: BAU creates a great deal of value; it is how the organisation earns its living.
whyNot.2: BAU has plenty of targets (service levels, output volumes), so this is false.

B.q:
Which THREE of the following are typical of business as usual?
1) Permanent functional teams
2) Repetitive tasks
3) Delivering a unique output
4) Aiming for stability and efficiency
options: 1, 2 and 3
1, 2 and 4
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
B.why: BAU uses permanent functional teams (1), carries out repetitive tasks (2) and aims for stability and efficiency (4).

whyNot.0: Item 3 (a unique output) describes a project, not BAU.
whyNot.2: Item 3 is a project feature, so any option including it is wrong.
whyNot.3: Item 3 is wrong, and item 1 (permanent teams) is missing although it is typical of BAU.

B.q: A hospital installs a robotic dispensing system in its pharmacy. Once it is live, pharmacy staff use it every day. How is that daily use classified?
options: Still the project, as the robot is new
Business as usual, as it is now routine
A programme, as it involves several teams
A portfolio, as it supports the strategy
B.why: After transition, using the robot is repetitive, ongoing work by the permanent pharmacy team: business as usual.

whyNot.0: The project ended when the robot was handed over; how new the equipment is does not matter.
whyNot.2: A programme coordinates related projects and BAU for benefits; daily dispensing is not one.
whyNot.3: A portfolio is the organisation's whole collection of projects and programmes, not a daily task.

B.q: Where are most of the benefits of a project usually realised?
options: During the project's main delivery work
At the project's very first decision gate
In BAU, once the outputs are being used
When the business case is first approved
B.why: Benefits come from using the outputs, which happens in BAU after the project has handed them over.

whyNot.0: During delivery the outputs are still being built, so they are not yet in use.
whyNot.1: The first decision gate decides whether to continue; no outputs exist yet.
whyNot.3: Approving the business case authorises the work; it does not deliver any benefit.

C.q: Which statement about risk in projects and business as usual is correct?
options: Projects carry more risk, because their work is unique
BAU carries more risk, because it continues with no end
Projects carry less risk, because they are fully planned
Both carry equal risk, because both consume resources
C.why: Unique work has no exact precedent, so projects carry more uncertainty than the practised routines of BAU.

whyNot.1: Being ongoing does not make BAU riskier; its repetition makes it well understood and lower risk.
whyNot.2: Planning helps, but cannot remove the uncertainty that comes from doing something new.
whyNot.3: Using resources is common to both and says nothing about their relative risk.

C.q: A retailer's IT team applies the same security update to every till each month. A manager wants to run this as a project. Why is that unsuitable?
options: It is too small to need any planning
It is routine and repeats with no end
It is not linked to company strategy
It does not have its own named sponsor
C.why: The work is repetitive and ongoing with no defined finish, which makes it business as usual rather than a project.

whyNot.0: Size is not the test: small one-off jobs can be projects.
whyNot.2: BAU supports strategy too; strategic links do not decide whether work is a project.
whyNot.3: Lacking a sponsor is a symptom, not the reason; the work is simply routine.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a genuine difference between projects and business as usual?
options: Projects are temporary; BAU is ongoing
Projects are unique; BAU is repetitive
Projects deliver change; BAU sustains it
Projects have a budget; BAU has none
C.why: Both projects and BAU have budgets, so this is not a real difference. The other three are the classic contrasts.

whyNot.0: Temporary versus ongoing is a genuine difference.
whyNot.1: Unique versus repetitive is a genuine difference.
whyNot.2: Change versus sustaining current operations is the most fundamental difference of all.

reteach.title: Refitting the kitchen vs cooking dinner
reteach.question: A family has a new kitchen fitted over three weeks. After that, someone cooks dinner in it every night. Which is the project, and which is business as usual?

blocks.h: The refit changes things; dinner keeps things going
blocks.body: The kitchen refit is the project: a one-off, with a start and finish, a temporary team (fitter, electrician, plumber), a budget and some uncertainty (what's behind that wall?). Cooking dinner every night is business as usual: repetitive, ongoing, done by the household, and low risk because they know how. The refit is worth doing because of the better dinners that follow.

blocks.text: Don't be fooled by importance or frequency. Feeding the family is vital, and the annual boiler service happens rarely, but both are routine. Only the one-off change (the refit) is the project.

explain.body: BAU is the steady-state work that keeps the organisation running: repeated, ongoing and done by permanent teams. Ask: does this happen over and over in much the same way, with no planned end? If yes, it is BAU.

test.q: Which of the following is an example of business as usual?
options: Relaunching the company's website
Merging two regional sales offices
Introducing a new staff uniform
Processing customer refunds daily
test.why: Processing refunds every day is repetitive, ongoing work by a permanent team: BAU.

whyNot.0: A website relaunch is one-off change with an end date: a project.
whyNot.1: Merging two offices is a unique, time-bound change: a project.
whyNot.2: Introducing a new uniform is a one-off change; wearing it afterwards is BAU, but introducing it is a project.

explain.body: Projects are temporary, unique, change-making, higher risk and staffed by temporary teams. BAU is ongoing, repetitive, stability-seeking, lower risk and staffed by permanent functional teams. Exam distractors often swap a pair round, so read each side carefully.

test.q: Which pairing correctly contrasts a project (first) with business as usual (second)?
options: Repetitive work vs unique one-off work
Ongoing work vs time-bound work
Temporary team vs permanent team
Seeking stability vs making change
test.why: Projects use temporary teams that disband; BAU is run by permanent functional teams.

whyNot.0: This is reversed: projects are unique and BAU is repetitive.
whyNot.1: This is reversed: projects are time-bound and BAU is ongoing.
whyNot.3: This is reversed: projects bring change and BAU seeks stability.

explain.body: Projects and BAU share plenty: both use people and money, both have targets, both need managing and both serve the organisation's goals. That is why options built on 'projects have X, BAU doesn't' (budgets, deadlines, benefits) are usually wrong.

test.q: Which feature do projects and business as usual usually share?
options: Both need resources and a budget
Both are unique and one-off work
Both have a defined finish date
Both exist mainly to make change
test.why: Both projects and BAU consume people, money and materials, so both need resources and a budget.

whyNot.1: Only projects are unique; BAU is repetitive.
whyNot.2: Only projects have a defined finish; BAU is ongoing.
whyNot.3: Only projects exist to make change; BAU sustains current operations.

explain.body: A project ends by transitioning its outputs into BAU. The operational teams then run and use them, and the benefits flow from that everyday use. The project team disbands; BAU carries on.

test.q: A project builds a new customer portal. Who will usually run it day to day after handover?
options: The project team, for good
The BAU operational teams
The organisation's auditors
The project sponsor alone
test.why: After transition, the permanent operational (BAU) teams run and use the outputs; the project team disbands.

whyNot.0: Project teams are temporary and disband when the project closes.
whyNot.2: Auditors check compliance; they do not run services.
whyNot.3: The sponsor is accountable for the benefits but does not personally run the portal day to day.
